raw_comment: Something I noticed was that Trump seems to win by a landslide based of area of influence alone, because almost all of the map is painted red in his support. I know however, that he lost the popular vote by a little bit, which means that a large majority of the population must live in these smaller, more liberal areas. Despite this, I wonder how nearly half of the country can live in such a small area. I know California is by far the most populous state, but areas like Northeast Arizona and Northwest New Mexico surprised me because they do not strike me as being particularly populated nor in favor of Hillary. I also wonder why the blue areas are so separated while the red areas are much more conjoined. A title for this graph could be "Half is Less Than You Think." My idea behind this title is that the blue represents about half of the nation, and yet it doesn't appear to be close to half of 350 million people. The article could go into voting statistics and explain why this graph might appear inaccurate. That is what I think is going on in this map.

raw_comment:
Welcome to “What’s Going On in This Graph?” and the Wednesday moderation.  Today’s graph is a heat map showing the voting results from the 2016 presidential election by U. S. voting precincts. 
For comparison, you can look at this national map detailing 2018 House election results (https://tinyurl.com/2018ByDistrict).  
And you can see how your area (https://tinyurl.com/2016ByPrecinct) or even neighbors (https://tinyurl.com/2016Neighbors) voted in 2016 by entering any address, ZIP code, or town or city.  
Study the maps and statistics and, from 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, give us your responses online to these three questions. (On Thursday afternoon, we’ll reveal the articles that included these graphs and much more.) 

	What do you NOTICE in these graphs? 

	What do you WONDER? What are you curious about?

	What’s GOING ON in these graphs? 
Write a catchy headline that captures the graphs’ main idea.  If your headline makes a claim, tell us what you noticed that supports your claim.

The questions are intended to build on one another, so try to answer them in order. Start with “I notice” and then “I wonder,” and end with the headline.

Then, read some responses. Click on "Reply" to an interesting response to get a discussion going. Learn different perspectives when you read what other students have to say about your response. 

We look forward to reading your discoveries.

raw_comment: The first thing I noticed about this graph is that red completely dominates the entire country. But, in my town, and on the east coast of Massachusetts in general, Hilary Clinton had the majority of the votes. In my precinct in particular, she had 52% of the votes, while Trump only had 39% of the votes. Massachusetts appears to be the state with the highest percentage of Hilary supporters, and New England in general seems to be the region that supports Hilary the most. But, while all counties in Massachusetts voted the majority for Hilary Clinton, there are some towns that voted for Trump. In fact, in one of the towns adjacent to my own, Donald Trump received 52% of the votes. This leads me to wonder how two towns that are so close and so similar can have completely different outcomes in their election results. raw_comment: Where I live, Hampstead, New Hampshire, voting follows the national trend in supporting Trump. In my town, 58% of voters or 3,186 people voted for Donald Trump while 36% of voters or 1,996 people voted for Hilary Clinton. However, if you travel south for about 20 minutes, the area begins to favor Hilary Clinton by a larger majority. In Lawrence, Massachusetts, where a large population of Hispanic and Black voters lives, Hilary is favored to 86% over Trump’s 10%. My question is this: should we consider the electoral college outdated? Wouldn’t it make sense for majority votes to dictate the outcome of elections? This map is meant to physically illustrate how the country tended to vote during the 2016 Presidential Election. The discoloration on the graph is there to indicate which states, regions, and towns voted for which primary candidate, and how popular the candidate is in the recorded data.   If I was to create a title for the map shown, “America Is More Purple Than We Are Led to Believe” seems to be the most fitting. Since popular vote was in favor of Clinton (by a small margin), but the electoral college votes tilted towards Trump, America is in a time of political separation; there are seemingly equal amounts of people that support each candidate in each party, it’s just that distribution of the votes that create a majority “red” map.

raw_comment: The first thing I noticed was how dominant the color red was. It seems as though the majority of the people in the U.S. are Republicans, but that's not true. One can see that the East Coast and the West Coast have a more dominant presence of the color blue than the rest of the country, as well as lower Texas and parts of New Mexico, where it is obvious that there are a good amount of Democratic supporters. As you zoom in, I think it's important to see that there are parts of the states that seem to be in complete support of the Republican, which was Trump at the time, that are in support of Hilary who was the Democratic campaigner. I wonder why the creators of the map decided to make a state completely red, even when there were cities within that state that were blue. I think it's important to not only show a state's majority but also the minority. I also wonder why the East Coast and the West Coast favored Hilary and the rest of the country supported Trump. What factors were involved? Was religion involved? If it was, does one specific religion only support one side? As I zoom in to where I live, my town and the surrounding area is mostly blue. As you get closer to NH it becomes predominately red. I live on the border of MA and NH, so my town voted 48% (Trump) and 42% (Hilary). It's interesting to see how the closer you get to certain states, the more the votes vary and favor one campaigner over the other. My headline would be, "The Truth Lies Beneath the Tip of the Iceberg"

raw_comment: The first thing I noticed when I first looked at the map was that it appears that the red areas, which are areas that voted Republican, seem to dominate the map of the country. Then my eye started to gravitate towards the Massachusetts area and I noticed that it was blue, and the states directly North and South of Massachusetts seem to create this blue line down the Eastern coast of the country that stops and curves above Florida and continues West until Alabama. I began looking for other blue areas and I noticed that the West coast (California and Washington) seems to follow a similar trend, skipping over Oregon. I then searched for how my town and the surrounding towns voted and found that they mostly voted for Clinton, with my town divided 63% for Clinton and 27% for Trump. The map showed me that the closest Trump area to my town was Peabody, about a 17-minute drive away. It was interesting to see how my town voted compared to the state and to the entire country. Something that I wondered was how the election results were so close when the map seems to depict such a large gap between Trump voters and Clinton voters. If I were to write a headline for this map, it would be “The Importance of Zooming in on the Bigger Picture” because the story this map is telling is that Trump swept the country, however in reality we know that the win was actually quite narrow.

raw_comment: When I first opened the map I immediately said, "Wow...I had no idea that much of the country voted Republican."  I noticed that Democratic voters were a rarity which suprised me because the majoirty of people who surround me are Democratic.  This proves that I do live in a political bubble because I was surprised to see the map the way it is.  As the map zoomed into my town, Swampscott, MA, it got overwhelmingly more blue. ## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Geographic location / region | Spatial / geographic | Position on map; polygon boundaries |
| Unnamed numeric value | Quantitative (likely diverging) | Fill color/hue of polygons (blue to red, with lighter tones near midpoint) |
| State / place names | Categorical/nominal | Text labels on map |

### Notes
- No visible x- or y-axes are shown; spatial position is determined by the map projection.
- No legend is visible in the provided image, so the quantitative variable cannot be named from the image alone.

raw_comment:
As I look closely at the interactive map, I notice that primarily the country is red, but when you zoom in closely to where I live it is mostly blue.  Also, it is interesting to see that some neighboring towns, cities, or states are colored differently.  For example, it was a landslide for Clinton in Lawrence, but in Pelham, NH Trump won by a majority.  Other suburban towns, like my hometown, Andover,  voted for Clinton, but not as strongly.   I cannot help but wonder why these  communities voted so differently given their geographic proximity.   Is it related to average income, presence of children, average age, ethnic background?  The map coloring does not tell the full story.  Also, I'm curious how this map changed during the course of the election related to polling.  Was it accurate?  And how did the Democratic/Republic vote in this election compare with last presidential election.  Did people vote candidates or party?  This map does not give a good representation and the color coding is misleading to what happened during the election because we know it was roughly equal during the time of the election

raw_comment: According to the New York Times “An Extremely Detailed Map of the 2016 Election”, the region where I live in Marblehead, Massachusetts, is clearly a “Clinton precinct”, with 61% of the 1,858 total votes for Hillary, and only 31% of the votes for Trump. It interests me that more coastal areas such as Marblehead, Beverly, and Manchester contain the most Hillary supporters. The nearest “Trump Precinct” to me is in South Peabody, which is further inland. I can’t help but wonder why there is a greater amount of Hillary supporters on the coast. This trend pertains to more than the New England north shore - it can be seen along the coast of California as well. Perhaps the voting trends relate to the demographics of people who inhabit certain areas of the country. After all, citizens from different areas of the US are bound to want different things from their president due to the geographical, social, and economic landscapes that surround them. I would like to know what these general, regionally determined desires might be. Overall, this map exhibits that  US citizens of the middle states were all in favor of Trump, possibly because his campaign arguably promised more social, political, and economic change than Hillary's did. If I was to create a headline for what this map displays, I would probably title it “Middle States Vote In Favor of Change”, due to the previously mentioned connotations of Trump's campaign.
